the administration of chlrotetracycline and tylosin at subtherapeutic levels in the feed of swine had no effect on the growth rate of swine, but the continuous feeding of tylosin-supplemented feed increased the incidence of tylosin resistance in the intestinal microbiota and the fecal concentration of the resistance determinant erm(B).
the subtherapeutic use of tylosin, but not chlortetraclycline, increases the resistance to these antibiotics in the gut of pigs.

the impact of subtherapeutic use of tylosin on the emergence and persistence of antimicrobial resistance in swine.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the administration of subtherapeutic levels (11-44 and 5.5 ppm, respectively) of tylosin or chlortetra-cycline in swine production did not have a positive impact on growth rate.

the use of tylosin at subtherapeutic levels in the feed for the purpose of increasing growth rate in pigs results in the development of resistance to tylosin and to other macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin B antibiotics, as well as the development of erm(B) resistance.

the administration of subtherapeutic levels (i.e., 11-44 ppm for 3 weeks) of tylosin in swine feed can result in increased resistance to tylosin in the intestinal microbiota and the selection of erythromycin-resistant strains, but the continuous administration of chlotetracycline-supplementation at 5.5 ppm in swine feed had no significant impact on resistance to chlortetraycline in the intestinal microbiome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
subtherapeutic levels (i.e., below the therapeutic level) of tylosin, when fed to swine, can increase the prevalence of tylosin resistance in anaerobic gut flora.

subtherapeutic administration to pigs of antimicrobial agents, such as tylosin, can result in the rapid selection and dissemination of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria, even when the antimicrobial agent is withdrawn.

tylosin supplementation of swine feed at a subtherapeutic level for 12 weeks resulted in a significant increase in the prevalence of tetracycline resistance in fecal samples, while chlortetraclyne supplementation had no significant effect.
